Newborn Mastomys natalensis pups are remarkably altricial, weighing a mere 2.4 grams [Wwb = 2.4 grams] at birth, a value that underscores the significant energetic investment required for the subsequent rapid development of the offspring. Litter sizes in this species are notably large; females typically produce an average of 3.9 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.9 pups per litter], a fecundity that contributes to the species' reputation as a prolific colonizer of disturbed habitats across sub-Saharan Africa. This high birth rate is a key component of their life history strategy, allowing populations to recover swiftly after seasonal declines or periods of intense drought. The consistent availability of resources within grain stores and human settlements, where the species is often considered a pest, appears to support these large litters and the subsequent high maternal investment in lactation and pup rearing.

Field studies indicate that under favorable conditions, female Mastomys natalensis can achieve a remarkably high reproductive output. They are capable of producing approximately 0.67 litters per month [F_R_i = approximately 0.67 litters per month] during peak breeding seasons, a frequency that, when combined with the large litter sizes, drives explosive population growth. This impressive rate of reproduction is facilitated by a relatively short gestation period of 23 days [tg = 23 days] at a core body temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This rapid gestation is characteristic of small murid rodents and allows females to quickly cycle through pregnancies in succession, maximizing their lifetime fecundity in environments where the window for successful breeding may be narrow, dictated by ephemeral rainfall and subsequent food availability. The synchrony between female reproductive cycles and environmental pulses is critical for population persistence.

The period of dependency in this species is brief, accelerating the population turnover. Weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence, occurs at 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This rapid weaning age allows the mother to redirect energy reserves toward her next reproductive effort with minimal delay. Young juveniles then experience a period of rapid somatic growth, though their development toward reproductive competence proceeds more slowly. Puberty, defined by the onset of the first oestrus or the production of viable spermatozoa, is not reached until 112 days after birth [tp = 112 days after birth] at 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This pre-reproductive period of over three months represents a significant phase during which individuals must acquire substantial body mass and develop the physiological capacity to support gestation and lactation.

The ultimate wet weight of a healthy adult Mastomys natalensis averages 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams], a body size that places it in the medium range for its subfamily. Reaching this asymptotic mass requires a consistent food supply; individuals in marginal habitats may never attain this size, consequently exhibiting reduced fecundity or delayed maturation. Life history theory predicts that the combination of a 40-gram adult body mass with the species' high reproductive rate should correspond to a relatively short lifespan, constrained by the trade-off between current reproduction and somatic maintenance. Indeed, field and laboratory records consistently document a maximum lifespan of 840 days [am = 840 days] when individuals are maintained at a constant 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This longevity of just over two years is typical for a small mammal of this size and reproductive tempo, with most free-living individuals succumbing to predation, disease, or environmental stress well before reaching this upper limit.

Ecologically, the rapid population dynamics of Mastomys natalensis are a direct consequence of its finely tuned reproductive parameters. The high fecundity, characterized by a maximum litter size of 3.9 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.9 pups per litter] and a corresponding reproductive frequency of approximately 0.67 litters per month [F_R_i = approximately 0.67 litters per month], culminates in a daily reproduction rate that is sustainable only within a narrow thermal window centered on 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. Deviations from this optimal temperature, whether due to seasonal cold stress or heatwaves during the dry season, can delay the 23-day gestation period (23 days) [tg = 23 days] or increase pup mortality, thereby dampening population irruptions at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C]. This thermal sensitivity, combined with resource availability, explains the species' famous boom-and-bust cycles in East and Southern Africa. Conservationists track these cycles to predict outbreaks of Lassa fever, for which the multimammate mouse is the primary reservoir host, highlighting the direct human health implications of understanding these fundamental life history traits.
